# **Abstract**

Machine-learning models that make predictions from continuously arriving time-series data — such as electricity demand, financial transactions, or sensor readings — gradually lose accuracy as the underlying data changes over time. The usual remedy is to retrain the model, but current practice is crude: many systems retrain on a fixed timetable, which wastes computing power and energy on updates that are not needed, while others retrain the moment any statistical change is detected, over-reacting to routine seasonal patterns. Both extremes are costly, and every unnecessary retraining of a large model consumes electricity and produces avoidable carbon emissions. This project asks whether a smarter, cost-aware decision rule can determine not only when a model should be retrained but also how much effort that retraining should involve.

We propose to develop and test a decision policy that, at each moment, chooses among three actions: do nothing (skip), apply a small and inexpensive incremental update, or perform a full and more costly retraining. The policy will combine several signals that existing methods use only in isolation — statistical measures of how far the recent data has drifted from the past, an allowance for predictable seasonal variation so that normal cycles are not mistaken for genuine change, the model’s own performance and confidence, and the measured computational and energy cost of retraining itself — into a single score that recommends the most economical action that still protects prediction quality. The policy will be evaluated on large-scale time-series datasets against common baselines, including never retraining, retraining on a fixed schedule, and retraining whenever drift is detected. Success will be judged not by accuracy alone but by an explicit accuracy-versus-cost trade-off, measuring prediction quality alongside how often retraining occurs, how quickly genuine change is caught, and the energy used and carbon emitted. If effective, the resulting policy would let organisations keep predictive models accurate while substantially reducing the computation, cost, and environmental footprint of maintaining them — a practical contribution to sustainable, large-scale machine-learning operations.

Key words: concept drift; model retraining; energy-efficient ML; time-series; MLOps;

1. # **Introduction**  {#introduction}

Machine-learning models deployed on continuously arriving time-series data — electricity demand, financial transactions, sensor telemetry, retail sales — are built on the assumption that the future resembles the past. In practice the data-generating process shifts: input distributions drift, seasonal cycles wax and wane, and occasional shocks reshape the relationship between inputs and targets, so a model that was accurate at deployment silently decays. The standard defence is retraining, but deciding when and how to retrain is surprisingly unprincipled. Most production systems retrain on a fixed schedule (nightly, weekly) or whenever a drift alarm fires. The former wastes computation, energy, and human effort on updates that change nothing; the latter reacts to every statistical wobble — including ordinary seasonality — and can retrain far more often than necessary. Each unnecessary full retrain of a large model consumes non-trivial compute, electricity, and carbon, and adds operational risk. This project proposes to investigate a cost-aware, seasonality-adjusted decision policy that, at each point in time, chooses among three actions — skip retraining, apply a cheap incremental update, or perform a full retrain — by weighing drift evidence, model-performance signals, and prediction uncertainty against the measured cost of retraining itself. The central aim is a policy that triggers fewer needless retraining events yet protects predictive accuracy, achieving a better accuracy–cost (computation and energy) trade-off than fixed-schedule or drift-only strategies. If successful, the outcome would give practitioners a practical, measurable rule for sustainable model maintenance, reducing the compute and carbon footprint of long-lived ML systems without sacrificing reliability.

2. # **Literature Review**  {#literature-review}

Maintaining a deployed model under changing data draws on three bodies of work: how distributional change is detected in streams, how models are adapted once change is suspected, and how the computational cost of that adaptation is measured. This review examines each in turn, identifies the strengths and weaknesses of prior approaches, and concludes with the gap the project addresses.

1. ## **Concept drift and its detection in data streams** {#concept-drift-and-its-detection-in-data-streams}

Concept drift refers to changes over time in the joint distribution P(X, y) on which a deployed model relies, and it has been studied extensively in the data-stream mining literature (Gama et al., 2014; Lu et al., 2018). A widely used taxonomy distinguished real drift, where the conditional P(y | X) changes and directly harms predictions, from virtual drift, where only the input distribution P(X) shifts; it also characterises the temporal shape of change as sudden, gradual, incremental, or recurring (Gama et al., 2014; Webb et al., 2016). Recurring drift was especially relevant to time-series streams: seasonal cycles cause distributions to depart from and later return to earlier states (Gama & Kosina, 2014). A detector that cannot separate such periodic variation from genuine change will raise a false alarm every time a seasonal pattern begins, which is precisely the failure mode a retraining policy must avoid.

Detection methods fell into two broad families. Performance-based detectors monitor a running estimate of predictive error and signal drift when it degrades beyond an expected bound. DDM (Gama et al., 2004\) and its early-warning refinement EDDM (Baena-García et al., 2006\) tracked a streaming classifier’s error rate, while ADWIN (Bifet & Gavaldà, 2007\) maintained an adaptive window and detected change by comparing the means of its sub-windows with formal statistical guarantees. These methods were sensitive and well understood, but they presupposed that ground-truth labels arrive promptly — often untrue in deployment, where labels are delayed, costly, or never observed (a difficulty known as verification latency). Distribution-based detectors avoided this dependence by comparing a recent current window of inputs against a reference window using two-sample statistics: the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test, the Population Stability Index (PSI) common in industry, Jensen–Shannon divergence, and kernel Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) (Gretton et al., 2012). Rabanser et al. (2019) evaluated such methods empirically for detecting dataset shift and found that no single statistic dominated across shift types, and that dimensionality reduction before testing often helped. The key limitation across this family was scope: these detectors answered only whether the data had changed. They neither quantified the change’s impact on the model nor indicated what maintenance action, if any, was warranted — and their own computation, run continuously over high-volume streams, was itself a recurring cost that the literature rarely accounted for.

2. ## **Model-maintenance strategies under drift** {#model-maintenance-strategies-under-drift}

Once drift was suspected, responses were divided into passive and active adaptation (Gama et al., 2014). Passive approaches updated the model continuously regardless of whether drift had occurred, typically through online or incremental learners such as Hoeffding trees (Domingos & Hulten, 2000\) and their adaptive variants, or through ensembles that add, weight, and prune members as data arrives — for example SEA (Street & Kim, 2001), accuracy-weighted ensembles (Wang et al., 2003), Dynamic Weighted Majority (Kolter & Maloof, 2007), and Adaptive Random Forest (Gomes et al., 2017), many of them implemented in the MOA framework (Bifet et al., 2010). Passive methods adapted smoothly but paid a constant update cost and could drift with noise. Active approaches instead coupled a drift detector to a discrete adaptation step — most commonly retraining on recent data when an alarm fires. In practice the discrete step was treated as a single fixed mechanism, and the choice between a lightweight incremental update (warm-starting from current parameters, cheap but prone to catastrophic forgetting and error accumulation) and a full retrain from scratch (robust but expensive) was seldom made explicit or automated.

A smaller body of work questioned whether adaptation was always worthwhile. Žliobaitė et al. (2015) framed model updating as a cost-sensitive decision, arguing that an update should be performed only when its expected benefit outweighs its cost, and showing that indiscriminate updating can be economically irrational. This aligned with the MLOps and production-ML literature: Sculley et al. (2015) identified model staleness and unglamorous maintenance as major sources of hidden technical debt, and case-study surveys reported that teams commonly fell back on fixed retraining schedules or manual, intuition-driven triggers because principled alternatives were lacking (Paleyes et al., 2022). 

Against this background, existing cost-sensitive treatments generally pose a binary choice — update or not — and assume a single adaptation mechanism. They did not consider a graded action space in which a cheap incremental update is a distinct option from an expensive full retrain, nor did they combine seasonality-aware drift evidence, model-performance degradation, and prediction uncertainty into one decision.

3. ## **Cost- and energy-aware machine learning (Green AI)** {#cost--and-energy-aware-machine-learning-(green-ai)}

The computational and environmental cost of machine learning became a research concern in its own right. Strubell et al. (2019) quantified the substantial energy use and carbon emissions of training large models, and Schwartz et al. (2020) proposed Green AI, arguing that efficiency should be reported alongside accuracy as a first-class evaluation criterion rather than an afterthought. A supporting ecosystem of tooling made these costs measurable in practice: frameworks for systematic energy and carbon reporting (Henderson et al., 2020), estimation tools such as CodeCarbon and the ML CO2-impact calculator (Lacoste et al., 2019), Carbontracker for training-time forecasting (Anthony et al., 2020), and empirical studies of the carbon footprint of large-model training (Patterson et al., 2021). This literature, however, focused overwhelmingly on the one-off cost of a single training run, or on architectural and hardware efficiency. It paid little attention to the repeated cost incurred across a model’s deployed lifetime, where retraining may recur hundreds of times. Over that lifetime, the frequency of retraining is arguably a larger lever on total energy consumption than any single-training optimisation — yet it was rarely treated as a decision variable within a Green-AI framing.

4. ## **Gap analysis**

Taken together, these three strands of work remained largely disconnected. Drift-detection research reliably signalled that a distribution had changed but stopped short of prescribing a maintenance action, and on time-series streams it often could not distinguish seasonality from genuine drift. Model-maintenance research either adapted continuously through a fixed mechanism or, at best, made a binary cost-sensitive update decision, without a graded action space spanning skip, incremental update, and full retrain. Green-AI research made computational and carbon costs measurable but did not feed them back into the maintenance decision. No existing approach unified seasonality-adjusted drift metrics, model-performance and uncertainty signals, and the measured cost of retraining — including the cost of detection itself — into a single policy that selects among the three actions to optimize an explicit accuracy–cost trade-off. This is the gap the proposed project addresses.

3. # **Significance and Innovation**  {#significance-and-innovation}

   1. ## **Significance** {#significance}

Reliable, affordable model maintenance underpins any organisation that depends on continuously updated predictions, from electricity-demand and financial-risk forecasting to retail and industrial IoT. By converting drift monitoring from an alarm into a cost decision, the project targets a problem sitting at the intersection of model reliability, operating cost, and environmental sustainability. A policy that measurably reduces unnecessary retraining would lower the compute, energy, and carbon footprint of long-lived ML systems — an increasingly important concern as models proliferate — while preserving accuracy and reducing the operational load on data-science teams. The contribution is also methodological: it brings explicit decision-theoretic, cost-aware reasoning to MLOps model maintenance, an area currently governed largely by heuristics, and the resulting framework would be transferable across domains and model families. The work would interest researchers in data-stream mining, sustainable and Green-AI research, and MLOps, as well as practitioners responsible for production forecasting systems.

2. ## **Innovation** {#innovation}

The project’s novelty lies in unifying signals that prior work has treated separately. First, it combines seasonality-adjusted drift metrics with model-performance degradation and prediction uncertainty into a single retraining-decision score, rather than relying on drift detection alone. Second, it replaces the conventional binary “update or not” choice with a three-way action space — skip, incremental update, or full retrain — letting the policy match the strength of its response to the severity and nature of the change. Third, it treats the cost of maintenance, including the cost of the detection computation itself, as an explicit term in the decision, and evaluates outcomes with energy (kWh) and estimated CO2 as first-class metrics alongside predictive performance. This reframing of model maintenance as a cost-aware, seasonality-aware control policy is, to our knowledge, not addressed as a unified problem in the existing literature.

4. # **Research Proposal or Methodology** {#research-proposal-or-methodology}

This section outlines a proposed solution to the problem identified above — an adaptive, cost-aware maintenance policy — and describes how its effectiveness and efficiency would be demonstrated. Because the project is speculative, the aim is not a finished system but a plausible, testable design together with a rigorous evaluation plan. The following subsections set out the approach, methodology, conceptual framework, timeline, and expected dissemination and benefits.

1. ## **Approach (modify as applicable, remove if not applicable)** {#approach-(modify-as-applicable,-remove-if-not-applicable)}

## We propose a retraining-decision policy that runs alongside a deployed forecasting model and, at each decision point (for example, the end of each day or data batch), recommends one of three actions: skip (leave the model unchanged), incremental update (a short, warm-started fine-tune on the most recent window), or full retrain (rebuild the model from a larger historical window). The policy derives a single retraining-decision score from four groups of signals: (i) seasonality-adjusted drift metrics on the input distribution; (ii) the model’s recent predictive performance where labels are available; (iii) prediction uncertainty as a label-free proxy for degradation; and (iv) the estimated cost — compute time and energy — of each candidate action.

## The seasonality adjustment is the core novelty of the approach. Rather than comparing the current window directly against an immediately preceding reference window — which flags every seasonal transition as drift — the policy compares the current window against a seasonally aligned reference (the same phase in previous cycles) and against a deseasonalized residual series. Genuine drift then registers as change that persists after known periodic structure has been removed, sharply reducing false alarms on strongly seasonal streams.

## Conceptually, the decision score is a benefit-minus-cost comparison. For each action the policy estimates the expected reduction in prediction error, weights it by a value-of-accuracy term, and subtracts the action’s expected compute and energy cost; it then selects the action with the greatest net expected value, subject to a configurable cost budget. As summarised in Table 1, this reserves expensive full retrains for large, persistent, non-seasonal shifts, while minor or purely seasonal fluctuations trigger a skip or a cheap incremental update.

## *Table 1\. The three maintenance actions and the conditions under which the policy selects each.*

| Action | Triggered when | Relative cost and expected benefit |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Skip | Only seasonal or negligible non-seasonal change; performance and uncertainty within bounds. | No maintenance cost and no benefit — avoids wasted computation and energy. |
| Incremental update | Moderate, persistent non-seasonal drift, or early performance decline. | Low cost (short warm-started fine-tune); moderate, fast benefit; some risk of gradual forgetting. |
| Full retrain | Large, persistent, non-seasonal shift, or sustained performance loss. | High cost (rebuild from long history); largest and most robust benefit. |

## 

2. ## **Methodology (modify as applicable, remove if not applicable)** {#methodology-(modify-as-applicable,-remove-if-not-applicable)}

The policy would be evaluated on several large-scale, publicly available time-series datasets that exhibit pronounced seasonality and known or injectable distribution shifts — for example electricity load demand, retail and web-traffic demand, and environmental or air-quality sensor streams — supplemented with semi-synthetic streams in which drift of controlled type, magnitude, and timing is injected so that ground-truth change points are known.

Drift would be quantified over rolling reference and current windows using complementary two-sample statistics: the Population Stability Index (PSI) and the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test for individual features, and Jensen–Shannon divergence and kernel Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) for multivariate, distributional comparison. Each metric would be computed both against an adjacent reference and against a seasonally aligned reference, and the gap between the two would isolate the non-seasonal component of change that the decision score acts on.

Where labels arrive (possibly with delay), rolling forecasting error such as MAE, RMSE, or MAPE would supply the performance signal; where labels are absent, prediction-interval width or ensemble disagreement would provide a label-free uncertainty proxy. Cost would be measured directly — wall-clock training time and energy — and used both as an input to the decision score and as an evaluation outcome. The decision rule would first be implemented as an interpretable threshold-and-utility policy, with a cost-sensitive optimisation or reinforcement-learning variant explored as a stretch goal.

The proposed policy would be compared against four baselines drawn from current practice: (1) never retrain; (2) periodic full retraining on a fixed schedule; (3) drift-only retraining, which retrains whenever any detector fires, with no cost or seasonality awareness; and (4) always-incremental updating. All strategies would be run on the same streams under identical conditions and judged on a bundle of metrics rather than accuracy alone: prediction performance, number of retraining events, detection delay, false-alarm rate, cumulative computation time, energy consumption (kWh) and estimated CO2, and an overall accuracy–cost utility score that combines them. Energy would be measured with CodeCarbon and, where available, hardware power counters, so that the sustainability claim rests on measured rather than assumed figures.

3. ## **Conceptual framework (modify as applicable, remove if not applicable)** {#conceptual-framework-(modify-as-applicable,-remove-if-not-applicable)}

The policy operates as a closed monitoring-and-decision loop, repeated at each decision point (Figure 1): (1) ingest the latest data window; (2) compute seasonally adjusted drift metrics against aligned reference windows; (3) read the model’s recent performance and prediction uncertainty; (4) estimate the cost and expected benefit of each candidate action; (5) compute the retraining-decision score and select skip, incremental update, or full retrain; and (6) execute the chosen action, log its measured cost, and update the reference windows. Because the cost of detection is itself included at step (4), the framework governs not only how often the model is retrained but also how often and how expensively it is monitored.

| 1 Ingest the latest data window |
| :---: |
| ↓ |
| 2 Compute seasonally-adjusted drift metrics against aligned reference windows |
| ↓ |
| 3 Read recent model performance and prediction uncertainty |
| ↓ |
| 4 Estimate the cost and expected benefit of each candidate action |
| ↓ |
| **5 Compute the retraining-decision score  →  select SKIP / INCREMENTAL / FULL** |
| ↓ |
| 6 Execute the action, log its measured cost, update the reference windows |
| ↓ |
| **Loop repeats at every decision point  —  return to step 1** |

*Figure 1\. The monitoring-and-decision loop executed at each decision point. Because the cost of detection (step 4\) is part of the decision, the loop governs how often the model is monitored as well as how often it is retrained.*

5. ## **Dissemination of Results (modify as applicable, remove if not applicable)** {#dissemination-of-results-(modify-as-applicable,-remove-if-not-applicable)}

Results would be disseminated through a paper in the data-stream mining or sustainable-computing community and through an open-source release of the policy and its evaluation harness, so that other researchers and practitioners can reproduce the findings and apply the policy to their own streams. A reproducible benchmark of retraining strategies with integrated energy accounting would itself be a reusable contribution.

6. ## **National/international Benefits (remove if not applicable)** {#national/international-benefits-(remove-if-not-applicable)}

Reducing unnecessary retraining lowers both the operating cost and the energy and carbon footprint of the many production machine-learning systems that forecast demand, detect fraud, or monitor infrastructure. As such systems proliferate nationally and internationally, a general, measurable policy for economical model maintenance contributes directly to sustainable-computing goals and to the reliability of data-driven services, while lowering the barrier for smaller organisations to keep their models current within a limited compute budget.

5. # **Conclusions** {#conclusions}

This proposal aims to address the challenge of maintaining predictive models on constantly changing time-series data while avoiding unnecessary computational and environmental costs. Existing maintenance strategies often rely on fixed retraining schedules or immediate retraining upon drift alerts. These approaches can lead to updating the model when no substantial changes have occurred, or overreacting to transient and seasonal variations, respectively. This research will develop a decision-making strategy that considers seasonality and cost, allowing for a choice between three operations: no update, incremental learning, and full model retraining.

This strategy will integrate evidence from factors such as data distribution variations, recent predictive performance, model uncertainty, seasonal behavior, and estimated computational and energy costs. It will be evaluated on large-scale time-series datasets and compared to baselines with fixed schedules, drift triggering, and no retraining. Performance evaluation metrics include predictive accuracy, drift response latency, retraining frequency, computation time, energy consumption, and estimated carbon emissions. The anticipated outcome is a practical model maintenance framework that reduces unnecessary retraining while maintaining predictive reliability. More broadly, this research may contribute to improving the efficiency, economy, and environmental sustainability of machine learning in response to evolving data streams.
